scenes.title: A question from school
scenes.intro: In August 2026, more than a hundred years after the Somme, four of Henry's descendants went to find him.

stories.title: It started with homework
stories.body: One of Henry's great-great-granddaughters was studying the First World War at school and asked for a family trip to the Somme. A guide, an ex-soldier, was found to lead it.

stories.title: The first question
stories.quote: is there any family member who was in WWI
stories.body: When he heard about Henry, he built the whole trip around him.

scenes.title: In his footsteps
scenes.intro: The second day of the trip: the Somme.

stories.title: The Quadrilateral
stories.body: The guide read from the account of 1 July 1916. Then the six of them spread out across the field and walked, until the guide told them to stop. This was the ground Henry crossed with the Somerset Light Infantry, and where he was shot.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
stories.quote: We spread out across the field and walked until our Guide told us to stop.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: Little crosses
stories.body: They left little crosses at the grave of Henry's commanding officer, Lieutenant-Colonel Thicknesse, and at the grave of the only other man of the Somerset Light Infantry killed that day who has a named grave.

stories.title: Newfoundland Park
stories.body: At the Beaumont-Hamel Newfoundland Memorial they saw the original trenches, and how close the German trenches were, "just a matter of yards away". Today sheep and goats keep the grass short, and "the trenches look 'respectful'".

stories.title: The caribou
stories.body: The bronze caribou at Beaumont-Hamel looks out over the ground where the Newfoundland Regiment attacked on 1 July 1916. Most of the men who went forward that morning were killed or wounded. Newfoundland remembers 1 July every year.

stories.title: Next door to Henry
stories.body: The Newfoundlanders belonged to the 29th Division, whose memorial stone stands in the park. On 1 July the 29th Division attacked at Beaumont-Hamel, right next to Henry's 4th Division, a short walk to the north.

stories.title: Thiepval
stories.quote: so many names all over every inch of the monument
stories.body: The day ended at the Thiepval Memorial, where more than 72,000 men of the Somme with no known grave are named on its great piers, among them many of Henry's Somerset comrades. Below it, a small cemetery holds French and British soldiers side by side, their crosses and headstones facing each other across the lawn.

photos.caption: The grave of Lieutenant-Colonel J. A. Thicknesse, Henry's commanding officer, killed on 1 July 1916 aged 46. The family left this little cross and poppy.
photos.alt: A white headstone carved with the Somerset Light Infantry badge and the words Lieutenant Colonel J. A. Thicknesse, Somerset Light Infantry, 1st July 1916, age 46, with a cross and the line God proved them and found them worthy for himself. A small wooden cross with a red poppy stands in front.

photos.caption: What the fields still give up: helmets, shell fuses, barbed wire, bottles, tools and twisted metal, found on the battlefields and shown in a museum on the trip.
photos.alt: Tables and shelves crowded with rusted First World War finds: German steel helmets, shell nose-cones, coils of barbed wire, glass bottles, spades and corkscrew wire pickets.

photos.caption: The Quadrilateral field today.
photos.alt: A wide field on Redan Ridge.

photos.caption: Newfoundland Park, Beaumont-Hamel: the old trench lines are still there under the grass. Looking from the British side towards the German line by the trees.
photos.alt: Deep grassy zigzag trenches crossing a field, with a footpath and a single walker, and a line of trees beyond.

photos.caption: Across No Man's Land at Newfoundland Park. The humps and hollows are shell holes and trenches.
photos.alt: A wide field of dry grass, rippled with low humps and hollows, behind a rope fence, with a path leading to trees and a memorial.

photos.caption: Inside one of the grassed-over trenches.
photos.alt: Looking along a deep trench with steep grassy sides, towards a row of trees.

photos.caption: The caribou memorial to the Newfoundland Regiment.
photos.alt: A bronze caribou with its head raised, standing on top of a mound of rocks and shrubs against a blue sky.

photos.caption: The 29th Division memorial, with the division's red triangle. The 29th fought right next to Henry's division on 1 July 1916.
photos.alt: A rough granite boulder among trees, with a bronze plaque showing a red triangle and the words 29th Division 1914 to 1918.

photos.caption: Under the arches of the Thiepval Memorial, every stone face carved with names.
photos.alt: A man in a cap walks between huge stone piers covered in carved names, towards an archway that opens on to fields and blue sky.

photos.caption: The steps up through the great arch at Thiepval to the Stone of Remembrance.
photos.alt: A long flight of stone steps rising through a tall brick and stone arch, with visitors at the top beside a long stone block.

photos.caption: The Anglo-French cemetery below the memorial: French crosses on the left, British headstones on the right, and the Somme fields beyond.
photos.alt: A cemetery seen from above: rows of small stone crosses on the left and white headstones on the right, a tall stone cross between them, and rolling farmland beyond.

scenes.title: Vimy Ridge and Lorette
scenes.intro: On the third day the family went to Vimy Ridge, where the trenches and shell holes have been kept as they were, and to Notre-Dame de Lorette on the next ridge, where France buries its dead.

stories.title: A real trench
stories.body: They walked through preserved trenches, with fire steps and sandbagged walls, and saw how close the two front lines had been. A low hollow in the trench wall, the guide explained, was where men could light a small fire to warm their food.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright, page 5

stories.title: The ground remembers
stories.body: More than a hundred years on, the grass at Vimy still rises and falls over shell holes and old trench lines.

stories.title: The memorial
stories.body: The Canadian National Vimy Memorial stands on the ridge Canadian troops captured in April 1917. Henry did not fight here, but men of every army walked through trenches like these.

stories.title: Notre-Dame de Lorette
stories.body: Lorette is France's largest military cemetery, with tens of thousands of French soldiers buried around a basilica, many of them unknown. One stone reads "Ici reposent les corps de 4563 soldats inconnus": here lie the bodies of 4,563 unknown soldiers.

stories.title: Peoples, be united
stories.quote: Peuples, soyez unis ; hommes, soyez humains !
stories.who: Carved on the memorial at Notre-Dame de Lorette
stories.body: Words carved in stone at Lorette, in English: "You who pass by, as pilgrims near their graves, climbing their Calvary and its bloody paths, listen to the cry that rises from the slaughter: Peoples, be united; men, be humane!"

stories.title: The Ring of Remembrance
stories.body: Beside the cemetery stands the international memorial, a great ring carrying the names of about 580,000 soldiers of every nation who died in this part of northern France: British, French and German side by side, in alphabetical order, with no ranks. The fields near Frémicourt, where Henry was taken prisoner, are in this region too.

photos.caption: The Canadian National Vimy Memorial on Vimy Ridge.
photos.alt: Two tall white stone pylons of a memorial on the skyline, across a wide slope of dry grass, with three trees on the left.

photos.caption: Shell holes and trench lines still ripple the ground at Vimy, now grassed over.
photos.alt: Close-up of dry grass with small yellow flowers in front of a field of grassy humps and hollows, with a Canadian flag beyond.

photos.caption: A preserved trench at Vimy, with its fire step. The sandbags were remade in concrete so it would last.
photos.alt: A narrow trench with walls of grey concrete sandbags, a fire step and a gravel floor.

photos.caption: The basilica at Notre-Dame de Lorette, among the graves. Each French cross carries a name and the words "Mort pour la France".
photos.alt: A white stone church with a slate dome and bell tower under a deep blue sky, with rows of small white crosses on dry grass in front.

photos.caption: Row after row of French crosses at Lorette.
photos.alt: Four white crosses with name plates in the foreground, and thousands more in rows stretching away under tall trees.

photos.caption: Looking out from Lorette across the Artois plain, fought over from 1914 to 1918.
photos.alt: A line of white crosses on dry grass in front of a hedge, with a flat plain and distant wind turbines beyond.

photos.caption: "Here lie the bodies of 4,563 unknown soldiers."
photos.alt: A stone slab carved in French: Ici reposent les corps de 4563 soldats inconnus.

photos.caption: "Peoples, be united; men, be humane!"
photos.alt: Carved capital letters on a stone wall, a French verse ending Peuples, soyez unis; hommes, soyez humains.

scenes.title: The two fields
scenes.intro: The third day: Frémicourt, and Belgium.

stories.title: Ploegsteert
stories.body: The family went to Ploegsteert, where Henry served with the 1st Wiltshires in the bitter winter of 1916 to 1917.

stories.title: Where he was taken
stories.quote: it was the furthest one away
stories.body: Near Frémicourt and Beugnâtre the guide showed them two fields where Henry was most likely captured on 24 March 1918.

stories.title: The Pool of Peace
stories.quote: something beautiful out of something so horrible
stories.body: At Spanbroekmolen they saw the crater of one of the nineteen Messines mines, now a quiet pool among trees. Henry's battalion attacked close by on 7 June 1917, while he was in hospital.

photos.caption: One of the two fields near Frémicourt where Henry was most likely captured, on 24 March 1918. Today it grows sugar beet.
photos.alt: A wide field of green leafy crops under a blue sky, with a stubble field, a line of electricity poles and distant wind turbines beyond.

photos.caption: The Pool of Peace at Spanbroekmolen, near Messines: the crater of one of the nineteen mines blown on 7 June 1917. A small cross and poppy stand at the edge.
photos.alt: A large still pool ringed with trees, with water lilies near the bank and a wooden edge in the foreground.

stories.title: Tyne Cot
stories.quote: I have no words to add to this scene.
stories.body: The largest Commonwealth war cemetery in the world, on the slope of Passchendaele Ridge. It was about 38 degrees that day.

stories.title: A German cemetery
stories.quote: Still sad to see… they left families behind too.
stories.body: In contrast, it was dark.

stories.title: The Menin Gate
stories.quote: such a moving and proud moment for the three of us
stories.body: At the evening ceremony, four trumpeters played the Last Post. Three generations of Henry's family laid a wreath under the arch.

stories.title: The card on the wreath
stories.who: The family's wreath card, in handwriting
stories.body: The card read: "In Remembrance. L/Cpl Henry Bowles. With our love and grateful thanks for all you and your comrades did for us. Grateful you survived too." It was signed by his granddaughter, his great-granddaughter and two great-great-granddaughters.
stories.source: The family's wreath card, Menin Gate, August 2026

photos.caption: "Their name liveth for evermore": the Stone of Remembrance at Tyne Cot.
photos.alt: The words Their Name Liveth For Evermore carved in a long white stone, against a blue sky.

photos.caption: Tyne Cot, the largest Commonwealth war cemetery in the world, on the slope of Passchendaele Ridge. "Sooo big, sooo many graves."
photos.alt: Row upon row of white headstones in the shade of a tree, with fields stretching away beyond the cemetery wall.

photos.caption: The Cross of Sacrifice at Tyne Cot is built on top of a German blockhouse, captured in October 1917. Visitors had left poppy wreaths and small crosses.
photos.alt: A tall white stone cross with a bronze sword, standing above a stone wall with an inscription, poppy wreaths and small wooden crosses at its foot.

photos.caption: Graves of soldiers whose names are not known: "A Soldier of the Great War, Known unto God".
photos.alt: White headstones carved A Soldier of the Great War, two with a maple leaf, with flowers and a poppy, and a visitor looking on.

photos.caption: Inside Tyne Cot lie a few German soldiers too. A red candle burns on one German grave, in front of the wall naming nearly 35,000 British and Commonwealth men with no known grave.
photos.alt: A single small German grave marker with a red candle on top, in front of a long memorial wall of names.

photos.caption: The family's poppy wreath under the Menin Gate. The card reads "In Remembrance. L/Cpl Henry Bowles. With our love and grateful thanks for all you and your comrades did for us. Grateful you survived too."
photos.alt: A close-up of a red poppy wreath with a white card handwritten In Remembrance, L/Cpl Henry Bowles, followed by the message.

photos.caption: The wreath in place, below panels of names of men with no known grave.
photos.alt: A poppy wreath hanging on a rail below a stone wall carved with columns of soldiers' names.

scenes.title: A little to the right or left
scenes.intro: At Notre-Dame-de-Lorette, before the ring of 580,000 names, it all became very emotional.

stories.title: The bullet
stories.quote: If, on that first day of the Somme the bullet that wounded him had been just a little more to the right or left I would not be able to experience the things I have in my life so far.
stories.body: Everyone who comes after Henry exists because he came home.

stories.title: Never forget
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
stories.quote: So many gave their lives, so many were badly wounded, so many were gassed and had health problems for the rest of their lives, so many kept all these experiences to themselves. They did all this for the freedom we have today. This is something we must Never forget.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

scenes.title: Your memories
scenes.intro: This chapter is not finished. It is waiting for the people who knew him.
